name: Gutierre-Munoz
summary: A village on the Castilian meseta in Ávila province where Alfonso VIII died on 5 October 1214, two years after his victory at Las Navas de Tolosa.
overview: Gutierre-Muñoz is a small village in the province of Ávila, on the old droving road between Valladolid and Madrid.
Its place in history rests on a single day: Alfonso VIII of Castile died here of a fever on 5 October 1214 while travelling south to meet his son-in-law.

imageInfo.note: The village itself preserves no medieval fabric of note and is not depicted on Commons, so the article is illustrated with the nearest substantial medieval structure in the same province: the twelfth-century circuit of Ávila, the walls of the city whose bishop was among those killed at Alarcos in 1195 under the same king. The image shows Ávila, not Gutierre-Muñoz.

contentSections.title: Overview
paragraphs: Gutierre-Muñoz lies on the flat cereal country of the northern Ávila meseta, one of the many villages resettled during the eleventh- and twelfth-century repopulation of the land between the Duero and the Sierra de Gredos. It sat on a royal and droving road linking the Valladolid country with the passes toward Madrid, which is why a travelling king was there at all.

It has no castle, no famous church and no battle. Its entry in the record is a death: on 5 October 1214 Alfonso VIII of Castile died in the village, and Castilian chroniclers noted the place because of the man.

contentSections.title: The death of Alfonso VIII
paragraphs: The king was travelling south from Burgos toward Plasencia, where he intended to meet his son-in-law Alfonso II of Portugal, when he was taken with a fever on the road. He died at Gutierre-Muñoz on 5 October 1214, in his fifty-ninth year, having reigned since 1158 — one of the longest reigns in Castilian history, begun when he was three years old.

His body was carried north for burial at the Cistercian abbey of Santa María la Real de Las Huelgas outside Burgos, the house he and his queen, Eleanor of England, had founded in 1187 and which they had always intended as their mausoleum. Eleanor died less than a month later, and was buried beside him.

contentSections.title: Two years after Las Navas
paragraphs: The death came at the close of the most successful phase of Alfonso's reign. In 1195 he had been broken by the Almohads at the Battle of Alarcos, a defeat that cost Castile its southern frontier towns and shook the kingdom for a generation. In 1212, at the head of a coalition with Aragon and Navarre, he reversed it completely at the Battle of Las Navas de Tolosa, which opened the Guadalquivir valley to Christian conquest.

He did not live to exploit the victory. The two years between Las Navas and Gutierre-Muñoz were spent on frontier consolidation and dynastic diplomacy rather than on further campaigning, and the conquest of Andalusia fell to his grandson Ferdinand III a generation later.

contentSections.title: What followed
paragraphs: Alfonso was succeeded by his son Henry I, a boy of ten, under the regency of his sister Berenguela. Henry died in 1217 when a roof tile fell on him at Palencia, and the crown passed to Berenguela, who immediately resigned it to her son Ferdinand III.

That sequence — an old king dead on the road, a child king dead by accident, and a mother who took the throne in order to give it away — put Castile into the hands of the ruler who would take Córdoba in 1236 and Seville in 1248, and who united Castile and León permanently in 1230.
